findings.anchor: rig/lib/checks.js:100-121 validateDisposition, against AD-15 / §5.2 and AT-SHAPE-5
findings.detail: AD-15 and §5.2 state an executable binding "may not be `true`, `echo`, an empty command, `process.exit(0)`, or any equivalent generic-success stub," and AT-SHAPE-5 makes a "silent, or no-op executable binding" a nonzero coverage gap. validateDisposition enforces only `Array.isArray(disposition.argv) && argv.length > 0`, and no other module under rig/lib implements stub rejection (a search for `echo`, `process.exit(0)` and generic-success across rig/lib returns nothing). So `{kind:'executable', argv:['true']}` is accepted as an honest executable disposition. The convention branch is equally shallow: `/repository|repo-specific|service-specific|tailored|convention:/i` means the string "service-specific" is itself a sufficient reason, which is the generic boilerplate the case fails. §2.1 lists "generic success bindings" first among rejected approaches; the guard that would make that rejection real does not exist. No stub is shipped in the 115 current dispositions, so this is an unenforced control rather than a live fabrication.

The only way the suite interrupts an install is `opts.interrupt_after`, a parameter in shipped production code whose own comment concedes it: "`interrupt_after` is a test-shaped hook still shipped in production." AT-INSTALL-1 requires interruption by crash, interrupt, permission denial, or full disk; a truncation parameter cannot fail for those reasons, so the resume path is proved against a cooperative caller rather than a hostile environment. It is also a production lever: any caller of resumeInstall or the lint-format install path can stop an install partway and leave a complete:false manifest. AT-HD-12 exists to stop exactly this shape ("the adversarial oracle cannot become a happy-path simulator"), and it does not catch it. Additionally the AT-INSTALL-1 case never asserts the case's load-bearing claim — that policy status, the install line, and a run report refuse to call a partially applied control enabled — even though policy.js:268-287 implements that withholding and could be asserted directly.

findings.anchor: tests/advanced-oracle.test.js:616 AT-CI-1 and :935 AT-UNINSTALL-1 versus their §13 trace rows
findings.detail: Both cases are materially narrower than the contracts they are the primary evidence for, and the shortfall is in each case the assertion that carries the risk. AT-CI-1's row promises "Seed all six provider configs and deep-compare every unrelated user value after integration; then uninstall and assert the job is gone and every unrelated value survives byte-for-byte"; the test seeds one provider, substitutes `assert.match(after, /user-ci/)` and `assert.match(after, /rig/)` for the deep comparison, and performs no uninstall — so the removability of the job Rig inserts into the user's own pipeline, which AT-UNINSTALL-1 and D11 both depend on, is unproven at this seam. AT-UNINSTALL-1's row promises installation "across every surface at once" followed by removal; the test hand-writes a one-record legacy manifest and checks a single AGENTS.md block, leaving the hook, CI job, host configuration and user-global entry — and the explicit "deleting .rig/ and declaring the repository clean must fail" discriminator — unasserted.

findings.anchor: §1 "the installed copy is a managed file, so editing it is drift" versus rig/lib/apply.js:368 and rig/lib/onboarding-check.js
findings.detail: The one trust root is read from the target's own `.rig/trust/gate1.allowed-signers` at every verification (trust-root.js:17-32), and the design's stated mitigation for a substituted root is that editing it is detectable drift. No shipped check implements that detection: apply.js:368 seeds `.rig/sync-map.json` as `{ "groups": [] }`, so the exact-copy control compares nothing; onboarding-check's unapproved-write scan tests for the *presence* of unjournaled projections, not for content divergence of a managed file from its journaled digest. trust-root.test.js:41 asserts byte-identity only between the two source-repo copies, never the installed one. Gate 1 §9 already accepts the substituted-signer residual under D17/D19 and AT-PRESENCE-2 only requires that an additional planted list change nothing (which holds and is well tested), so the Gate 1 case is met — but the design should state the honest ceiling rather than name a detector that is not wired.

findings.anchor: §5.6 / AD-31 / §12.3(4) / Slice 14 versus tests/advanced-oracle.test.js:210 and rig/lib/catalog.js:174
findings.detail: Four places in the design require that "every D24-authored fragment declares itself Policy-grade generic baseline practice and explicitly says it is not tailored to the installing repository," and §5.6 makes a missing declaration a gate failure. The implementation forbids exactly that wording: catalog.js:174 KNOWN_AUTHORED_BOILERPLATE matches /generic baseline practice|not repository-tailored|not tailored to the installing repository/ and reports it as a "known boilerplate sentence" failure, and the AT-SHAPE-6 case asserts `doesNotMatch(text, /generic baseline|not repository-tailored|not tailored/i)` over every fragment. The code is the better reading of Gate 1 (that sentence repeated 115 times is the "repeated filler" AT-SHAPE-6 fails), but the design clause now instructs the opposite of what ships, and the 2026-10-18 amendment's supersession list covers payload, version, installation and traceability — not catalogue wording — so the conflict is not disposed of.

findings.anchor: §13 AT-LF-6 trace row and §14 slice verification commands naming non-existent test files
findings.detail: The design names test files that do not exist in the worktree. AT-LF-6's evidence cell cites "`advanced-lint-format-lifecycle.test.js` with `advanced-apply.test.js`" — the former is absent. §14's Verification blocks invoke `tests/advanced-install-manifest.test.js`, `tests/advanced-install-resume.test.js`, `tests/advanced-uninstall.test.js`, `tests/advanced-host-detection.test.js`, `tests/advanced-remediation.test.js`, `tests/advanced-distribution.test.js`, `tests/advanced-claims.test.js`, `tests/advanced-report-disclosure.test.js` and `tests/advanced-install-docs.test.js`, none of which exist. This is the precise trap §10 documents ("`node --test <missing-file>` prints `Could not find` and **exits 0**"): an operator running a documented slice command sees green. The release gate itself is safe — traceTargets captures only the first backticked file per row, every §13 primary target exists and must be in the signed manifest (check-advanced-spec.js:143-148) — so this is a documentation defect, not a gate hole.

findings.anchor: rig/lib/policy.js:194 loadActivePolicy versus :345 validatePolicyApproval and AD-20
findings.detail: AD-20 says both approval methods "produce one common, replay-resistant activation receipt," and AT-PRESENCE-1 prefers host-native. validatePolicyApproval can mint a host-native receipt (signer.method = 'host-native'), but loadActivePolicy refuses any receipt whose method is not external-sshsig with `policy_active_unverifiable` — so a successful host-native activation yields an active bundle that enforcement cannot load. The failure is closed, and no shipping entry point reaches the branch (nothing supplies `opts.verifyHostAttestation`; onboarding.js:168 refuses host-native outright), so there is no user-visible defect today. But the host-native path exists as an injectable library seam whose only exercise is a test that supplies `() => true` as the verifier, which means AT-PRESENCE-1's preferred path is asserted against the test's own logic rather than a shipped one.

sandbox.js establishes isolation by running a probe inside the sandbox that must fail to write outside and must fail to connect to a reachable listener, and reports an unavailable sandbox with a named reason otherwise — a model of not claiming an unprovable guarantee. networkIsolationPrefix, which backs AT-LF-22 on the lint-format task path, accepts the weaker evidence that the wrapper merely exits 0 on an empty child; it never confirms the profile actually denies a connection. On Linux `unshare --net` makes this sound by construction, but on darwin the conclusion rests on NETWORK_SANDBOX_PROFILE being correct rather than on an observation. Relatedly, the AT-LF-22 case asserts only that the probe file is absent and not which status was returned, so it is green both when isolation denied the connection and when nothing ran.

findings.detail: Recorded so the receipt is not read as more than it is: Bash was unavailable in this session, so I could not run `git status`/`git diff` against origin/qa-prod, could not confirm the stated implementation digest or the 2672-file count, and could not execute `ssh-keygen -Y verify` to confirm that the modified `wiki/gate1/gate1.sig` verifies over the current (also modified) business-spec.md, acceptance.md and testing-infrastructure.manifest bytes. Every verdict above rests on reading the shipped modules and the manifested tests. AT-GATE-2's ordering and arming logic are verified by inspection; its signature validity for this candidate is not, and it remains a release precondition to re-run `npm test` on the exact candidate bytes.
